doc.title: Johnny Varro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Few young black players in mainstream jazz
summary: Varro recalls mixed bands and speculates black players resent the style's pre-Civil Rights associations.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: When I look at the players that excel at this kind of music, I don’t know what we want to call it, but I guess classic or mainstream.

I don’t see many young black players coming up. Now there seems to be a lot of younger white guys who are a generation below you I guess that are embracing the style. And I’m wondering why. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

It’s very sad. I’m very sorry to hear that because as I was saying, years ago when I played this music I was a young kid. And a lot of young kids, there was Johnny Windhurst, Bob Wilber, Kenny Davern, a young crop of musicians playing and we’d be playing with mixed bands like crazy. I mean I’d be — I was on a band once where I was the only white kid in the band. There was Jonah Jones on trumpet, Coleman Hawkins on tenor, Benny Green on trombone, Jo Jones on drums, various bass players, Gene Ramey maybe on bass and myself, the young white hope. And it was a great education. And then most of the bands were always mixed. Condon always had a mixed band, and it was delightful. It was a lot of fun to play and you got to learn with each other and drink from the same jugs and smoke the same cigarettes and do all that stuff. I mean it was a camaraderie there. I think it has something to do with the style, the times. This music relates to a time when things were rough for the black person, not necessarily the black musician, but the black person in the Civil Rights, this would be pre-Civil Rights I guess. And I think they resent the style of the music and they just don’t want to have any part of it. It kind of reminds them — this is just my own sermon.
I think it’s a good opinion.

I’m surmising this myself on my own, I don’t know whether I’m right or wrong. I think it is. I’ve thought about it and I think it’s sad. Because like you say I just don’t see too many black players playing this style of music. I can’t think of any. I mean I see some of the old timers that are still around like Joe Wilder and Jackie Williams, of course Milt Hinton just passed away but he was part of it. I played with him back in the 50s. But I wish there were more. John Lamb I played with here with Buster Cooper the other day. And it was great. Great to see a mixed band there. I was delighted.
